Sitkoff† There is broad consensus that the law of conflict of trust laws is outdated. Both the American Law Institute and the Uniform Law Commission have initiated reform projects to address this obsolescence. But there is no consensus around what went wrong or how to fix it. This Article, prepared for a Symposium on Conflict of Laws in Trusts and Estates, responds to that gap by providing a historically, theoretically, and institutionally grounded account of the rise and fall of the old regime with an eye toward informing ongoing law reform efforts. We first show that the prevailing regime—that of the 1971 Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws—was purpose-built to encode then-common norms of trust law and practice. We then explain how and why modern trust law and practice has departed from those norms, upending the Restatement’ s foundational assumptions. In the Restatement’ s era, conflicts of trust laws rarely arose and were easily resolved through reliance on the locational anchors of land, probate, and court supervision. Today, by contrast, provoking a conflict of trust laws by drafting a trust to capture the benefits of interstate variation in law is a routine estate planning strategy, and the locational anchors of land, probate, and court supervision have become unmoored. Indeed, our account recasts nearly every significant development affecting trust law and practice over the past fifty years as a contributor to the revolution in conflict of trust laws. Informed by this understanding of the old regime’ s obsolescence, we offer tentative suggestions for the law reform efforts currently underway. I. I NTRODUCTION The rules governing conflict of trust laws have never been more i m p o r t a n t . S t a t e t r u s t l a w h a s b e c o m e i n c r e a s i n g l y d i f f e r e n t i a ted on a growing number of salient issues. Billions of dollars in trust assets have moved to exploit these differences,1 an estate planning trend dependent on assumptions about how courts w ill resolve disputes involving a conflict of trust laws.2 Yet there is broad consensus that the prevailing legal regime for resolving such conflicts—that of the 1971 Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws (Second Restatement)—is no longer up to the task. Although there is consensus that the existing infrastructure for resolving conflicts of trust laws (we will use “trus t-conflicts” as a shorthand) is unequal to the demands of modern trust practice, we lack a historically, theoretically, and institutionally grounded account of how and why the existing regime went stale.5 This Article responds to that gap. Our principal contribution is to provide an understanding of the rise and fall of the old regime with an eye toward informing the ongoing law reform ef forts. W e proceed in three Parts. First, we describe the Second Restatement’s trust provisions and show how they were purpose-built by the leading trust scholar of the era, Professor Austin Wakeman Scott of Harvard Law School, to fit th eir moment. The trust provisions’ painstakingly detailed scheme of issue-by- issue rules—dividing trusts of land from trusts of personal pro perty (“movables,” in the Second Restatement’s jargon), dividing testamentary trusts from inter vivos trusts, and so on—are something of a misfit with the rest of the Restatement’s generally standards-based approach. The trust provisions are also overco mplicated, prescribing numerous categories that often yield the same or similar outcomes. Yet by codifying rule-based answers to trust-conflicts in accordance with locational anchors—land, probate, and court supervision—grounded i n t r u s t l a w a n d p r a c t i c e a t t h e time, the Second Restatement’s t r u s t provisions, even if overcomplicated, were good enough for that time. Trusts rarely crossed state lines and, even when they did, state trust laws seldom differed. So long as trust law and practice hewed to the model preserved in amber b y the Restatement, the Restatement would suffice to provide an answ er, albeit after a complicated categorization exercise, that accorded with trust practice in the era. Second, we explain how and why mode r n t r u s t l a w a n d p r a c t i c e departed from the model on which the Second Restatement is based. A variety of developments have led to more complicated trust arrangements that are today stressing Scott’s vintage rules beyond their tolerance points. Some of these developments are e xogenous to trust law and pract ice, including the geographic fragmentation of families, the shift in the nature of wealth from land to liquid financial assets, and the growth of a national financial market. Others are en dogenous, including the nonproba te revolution, the end of court supervision, the rise of the management trust, directed trusts, trust decanting, and—most importantly—diverging state laws fueled by the jurisdictiona l competition for trust funds. In consequence, trust-conflicts arise more frequently and in permutations unimagined by Scott’s rules with greater stakes for settlors, beneficiaries, planners, governments, and others. Crucially, the locational anchors on which the Second Restatement relies to resolve trust-conflict s problems when they do arise—l and, probate, and court supervision—have become unmoored. Half of Scott’s rules cover trusts of land and half again deal with testamentary trusts, and all presumed ongoing court supervision. That division and presumption cannot be squared with trust law and practice as it has developed since the Restatement. Land has been supplanted by liquid financial assets, wealth transfer through testamentary trusts has been supplanted by inter vivos trusts, and modern trust law and practice allow and even encour age trustees to stay out of court rather than submit to ongoing cou rt supervision. The overcomplicated rules of the Second Restatement no longer point to clear answers in view of these and related developments. Third, informed by our understanding of this revolution in conflict of trust laws, we offer some preliminary and tentative suggestions for the law reform efforts now underway. We advise reducing complexity by eliminating distinctions that no longer accord with practice reality or for which there is no longer a sound policy basis, such as between land and personal property and between testamentary and inter vivos trusts. We also advise fine-tuning the distinctions that remain, with a presumption against preserving differential categories with undifferentiated treatment. Many difficult questions remain and will be the continuing work of law reformers in the years to co me. II. T HE PREVAILING REGIME A. The Second Restatem ent’ s Trust Provisions The sixteen sections in the Second Restatement’s chapter on trusts are difficult to describe succinctly as they prescribe numerous rules with minor variations in outcome based on the nuances of the particular trust and issue at play. Although clear rules are often a benefit to estate planning, which tends to be prospective in nature, the complexity of the Second Restatement imposes the cost of requiring effort to distinguish among categories. In many cases this cost will come with little offsetting benefit, as the Restatement ultim ately treats so many of the di fferent categories the same or with only minor variation, in some cases calling for the application of an indeterminate standard.7 At a high level, the Second Restatement divides the world of trust- conflicts along three axes: first, it divides trusts of land from trusts of movables (i.e., personal property); second, among trusts of movables, it divides testamentary trusts from inter vivos trusts; and third, it divides based on the nature of the issue in dispute, prescribing distinct rules for interpretation, constr uction, validity, admi nistration, restrai nts on alienation, and powers of appointment.8 For each of these categories and issues, the Second Restatement prescribes choice of law based on, to varying degrees: the sett lor’s (express or implied) intent, the location of the property in tr ust, the settlor’s domicile, the “most su bstantially related” state to t he trust’s administration, state public policy, and still other considerations.9 6 . Trusts of Land Overcomplication for little benefit is perhaps most apparent in the sections addressing tr usts of land. Six different Second Restat ement sections on trusts of land all y ield the same re sult—the “situs r u l e ” — whereby the relevant law to apply is that which would be applied by the courts of the situs of the land. 10 The situs rule applies for issues of validity,11 administration, 12 court supervision of administration, 13 restraints on alienation,14 and the existence15 or exercise16 of a power of appointment. Yet each of these issues is addressed in its own standalone section. The only exceptions to the situs rule for trusts of land relate to issues of interpretation and construction,17 for which the Second Restatement defers to the settlor’s intent, albeit in different ways for ea ch. By building many distinctions without differences into the rules, while also encoding many slight differences based on nuanced categorical distinctions, the Restatement prescribed overly complicated rules with potentially costly and complex qu estions of categorization with out apparent offsetting benefits. Yet by codifying rule-based answers to trust- conflicts in accordance with locational anchors grounded in trust law and practice at the time, the Restatement would at least point to clear answers in accordance with those locational anchors, except, of course, on the topics for which those rules call for the application of an indeterminate standard. B. The Restatement’ s Trust Provisions’ Distinctive History and Approach The trust provisions of the Second Restatement are something of a misfit with the Restatement as a whole. This difference in appr oach reflects a difference in drafting history, as the Restatement’s t r u s t provisions were independently drafted by Professor Austin Wakem an Scott, the leading scholar of trust law in that era. The centerpiece of the Restatement is the potentially indeterminate and difficult to apply “most significant relationship” test. The trust provisions, meanwhile, prescribe 30. Id . § 273. 31. T HE REVOLUTION IN TRUST-CONFLICTS A revolution within and outside trust law and practice has upended the model on which Scott’s rules depended. Over the past several decades, trust-conflicts have become increasingly common and complex as state trust law has increasingly diffe rentiated and tr usts increasingly have connections to multiple states.
